text: Mange is very common, especially in pigs: its full 10–15 day life cycle happens on the animal, but it can survive up to about 4 weeks in wet soil; the adult female burrows tunnels just under the skin to lay eggs, causing intense scratching, vigorous rubbing, head shaking, and red blister-like lesions. Ticks feed only on blood (their mouthpart works like a harpoon), and heavy infestation can cause significant blood loss and weakness, especially in calves; their life cycle runs egg and larva in grass, then adult on the animal — an engorged female can swell to about 200 times her original size before dropping off to lay eggs and die, while new larvae wait in grass for their first blood meal from a passing animal. Flies (particularly a problem in pig farrowing/weaning pens) have a fast life cycle (7–14 days egg to egg-laying adult, with one female laying up to 400 eggs), making control difficult. Disease transmission by these parasites: flies can spread E. coli, Salmonella, Streptococcus, greasy pig disease (Staphylococcus), and Coccidiosis in pig farrowing pens, and horse flies can transmit Trypanosoma to cattle and horses; mosquitoes transmit Fowl Pox in chickens; ticks transmit Babesia and Anaplasma (local cattle are resistant, but imported/crossbred dairy cattle are at risk). Ticks on people (common where cattle are kept under the house, or where children handle cattle in the field) are painful and difficult to remove, cause strong irritation, and can transmit disease to humans too.
